Field notes 07 · 15 July 2026

Alignment completed

At head office, every room agreed with the new direction. The sites are still waiting to see what actually changes.

Another town hall speech: a senior leader from head office, excited about the new vision. The only question from the room is about parking.

He answers politely, finishes the tour, flies home, and reports: alignment completed. A week later, the programme is moving exactly as before.

It is easy to read the parking question as proof the site does not care. It is more useful to read it as data.

They were listening, mostly in their second language, to words made for boardrooms. Somewhere inside the speech there was a direction. They could not see what it changed for their site. They have seen new visions before. After each one, their work stayed the same. So they ask about something that is real now. Parking is real.

Some wait for authority that never arrives. They believe that moving without permission gets corrected. A town hall does not change what they are allowed to decide. Everyone waits for instructions from their own manager.

Others compare the new direction with the work they know and quietly conclude their current way is better. They may be right. They hold detail head office has never seen. No one asks, so it stays private.

None of this is defiance, and none of it means the message was wrong. A better speech would help only if it was built from the reality of each site, not just delivered to it. The two sides just check different things. At head office, the check is already done: every room agreed, the direction is launched. At the sites, the check is still running.

Did any deadline move?
Did any old project stop?
Can my manager approve something they could not approve before?

Nothing has changed, so nothing is real yet.

This is the moment the drift goes invisible. The direction lives in language, while the old system still decides the work. When I am called in, months later, the parking question is a funny story at head office. It was a signal, the first of many that no one could read.

There is a one-question test. A week after the session, ask each site lead: what can you do now that you could not do before the meeting? Listen for the pause, the careful sentence, the topic change. That answer means the session aligned the vocabulary, not the programme.

Anna Chodynicka, DRIFT Partners · First published 15 July 2026
